name: City life in the Inland Niger Delta at Jenne-jeno
summary: Jenne-jeno in Mali's Inland Niger Delta, settled from about 250 BCE, grew into a major urban and trading centre by 850 CE, the oldest known city of sub-Saharan Africa.
description: Jenne-jeno, in the floodplain between the Bani and Niger rivers in present-day Mali, was occupied from about 250 BCE by people who worked iron from the start. It expanded into a major urban centre by 850 CE and was the region's first known significant trading crossroads. The excavators found brick walls, a settlement hierarchy and long-distance trade but no sign of social stratification, and settlement was densest about 900 CE. The site was abandoned by 1400, after the town of Jenne had been founded nearby.

impact.note: One region, the Inland Niger Delta (reach 1); a major urban and trading centre was new there, but the excavation abstract reports unchanged subsistence and no social stratification, so the lower depth is taken (2, down from the lead's 3); the later town of Jenne nearby is the one successor the sources name (generativity 1).

date.label: by 850 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Jenne-jeno, populated as early as 250 BCE, had expanded into a major urban centre by 850 CE.

evidence.supports: Jenne-jeno (“Old Jenne”; Djenne-jeno), site of the oldest known city of sub-Saharan Africa, was populated as early as 250 B.C. and expanded to become a major urban center by 850 A.D.

date.label: about 900 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Settlement at Jenné-jeno reached its peak density about 900 CE, within a sequence that runs from 250 BCE to 1400 CE.

evidence.supports: The Inland Niger Delta (IND) site of Jenné-jeno is one of the longest Iron Age sequences in west Africa (250 B.C.-1400 A.D.), reaching its peak settlement density in 900 A.D.

date.label: by 1400 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Jenne-jeno had been abandoned by 1400 CE, leaving settlement mounds that hold the remains of the city.

evidence.supports: Abandoned by 1400, Jenne-jeno left behind tells (settlement mounds) containing the remains of a once-thriving city

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The date of first settlement (250 BCE; Phase I, 250 B.C. to 50 A.D. in the eHRAF abstract) is kept in the description and not as an event, so that the record is anchored on urban scale and not on first occupation.

The lead puts urban scale at c. 400 to 800 CE; the sources read say 'by 850 A.D.' and peak density in 900 A.D. Area and population estimates by phase and the city wall should be sourced from the McIntoshes' own publications.

The argument that this urbanism arose without outside stimulus or a ruling elite, and the earlier dry-stone settlements at Dhar Tichitt, were not checked; origin stays unknown until they are. Dia is not covered.
The eHRAF page is an abstract of the excavation report written by HRAF's indexers, not the report itself.
The coordinates of Jenne-jeno are from the supervisor's memory (about 3 km south-east of Djenné), not from a source. Check against a gazetteer.

research.note: The Met calls Jenne-jeno the site of the oldest known city of sub-Saharan Africa, but neither source examines whether its growth owed anything to cities north of the Sahara, so the lead's claim of independence is not established here.
